In [[mathematics]], a '''Brownian sheet''' or '''multiparametric Brownian motion''' is a multiparametric generalization of the [[Brownian motion]] to a [[Gaussian random field]]. This means we generalize the "time" parameter <math>t</math> of a Brownian motion <math>B_t</math> from <math>\R_{+}</math> to <math>\R_{+}^n</math>.

The exact dimension <math>n</math> of the space of the new time parameter varies from authors. We follow [[John B. Walsh]] and define the <math>(n,d)</math>-Brownian sheet, while some authors define the Brownian sheet specifically only for <math>n=2</math>, what we call the <math>(2,d)</math>-Brownian sheet.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Walsh|first1=John B.|title=An introduction to stochastic partial differential equations|date=1986|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|pages=269|ISBN=978-3-540-39781-6}}</ref>

This definition is due to [[Nikolai Chentsov]], there exist a slightly different version due to [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]].

== (n,d)-Brownian sheet ==
A <math>d</math>-dimensional [[gaussian process]] <math>B=(B_t,t\in \mathbb{R}_+^n)</math> is called a '''<math>(n,d)</math>-Brownian sheet''' if
* it has zero mean, i.e. <math>\mathbb{E}[B_t]=0</math> for all <math>t=(t_1,\dots t_n)\in \mathbb{R}_+^n</math>
* for the covariance function
::<math>\operatorname{cov}(B_s^{(i)},B_t^{(j)})=\begin{cases}
      \prod\limits_{l=1}^n \operatorname{min} (s_l,t_l) & \text{if }i=j,\\
      0 &\text{else}
    \end{cases}</math>
: for <math>1\leq i,j\leq d</math>.<ref>{{citation|arxiv=math/0409491|author=Davar Khoshnevisan und Yimin Xiao|date=2004|title=Images of the Brownian Sheet}}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

=== Properties ===
From the definition follows
:<math>B(0,t_2,\dots,t_n)=B(t_1,0,\dots,t_n)=\cdots=B(t_1,t_2,\dots,0)=0</math>
[[almost surely]].

=== Examples ===
*<math>(1,1)</math>-Brownian sheet is the Brownian motion in <math>\mathbb{R}^1</math>.
*<math>(1,d)</math>-Brownian sheet is the Brownian motion in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>.
*<math>(2,1)</math>-Brownian sheet is a multiparametric Brownian motion <math>X_{t,s}</math> with index set <math>(t,s)\in [0,\infty)\times [0,\infty)</math>.

=== Lévy's definition of the multiparametric Brownian motion ===
In Lévy's definition one replaces the covariance condition above with the following condition
::<math>\operatorname{cov}(B_s,B_t)=\frac{(|t|+|s|-|t-s|)}{2}</math>
where <math>|\cdot|</math> is the Euclidean metric on <math>\R^n</math>.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Lévy's Brownian motion as a set-indexed process and a related central limit theorem |first1=Mina |last1=Ossiander |first2=Ronald |last2=Pyke|journal = Stochastic Processes and their Applications|volume = 21|number=1|pages = 133-145|year=1985|doi=10.1016/0304-4149(85)90382-5}}</ref>

== Existence of abstract Wiener measure ==
Consider the space <math>\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\R)</math> of continuous functions of the form <math>f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R</math> satisfying
<math display="block">\lim\limits_{|x|\to \infty}\left(\log(e+|x|)\right)^{-1}|f(x)|=0.</math>
This space becomes a [[separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]] when equipped with the norm
<math display="block">\|f\|_{\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\R)} := \sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left(\log(e+|x|)\right)^{-1}|f(x)|.</math>

Notice this space includes densely the space of zero at infinity <math>C_0(\mathbb{R}^n;\mathbb{R})</math> equipped with the [[uniform norm]], since one can bound the uniform norm with the norm of <math>\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\R)</math> from above through the [[Fourier inversion theorem#Schwartz functions|Fourier inversion theorem]].

Let <math>\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathbb{R})</math> be the space of [[tempered distributions]]. One can then show that there exist a suitable separable [[Hilbert space]] (and [[Sobolev space]])
:<math>H^\frac{n+1}{2}(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R)\subseteq \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathbb{R})</math>
that is continuously embbeded as a dense subspace in <math>C_0(\mathbb{R}^n;\mathbb{R})</math> and thus also in <math>\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb{R})</math> and that there exist a probability measure <math>\omega</math> on <math>\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb{R})</math> such that the triple
<math display="block">(H^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb{R}),\Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb{R}),\omega)</math>
is an [[abstract Wiener space]].

A path <math>\theta \in \Theta^{\frac{n+1}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^n;\mathbb{R})</math> is <math>\omega</math>-almost surely 
* [[Hölder continuous]] of exponent <math>\alpha \in (0,1/2)</math>
* nowhere Hölder continuous for any <math>\alpha> 1/2</math>.<ref>{{citation|first=Daniel|last=Stroock|authorlink=Daniel Stroock|title=Probability theory: an analytic view|publisher=Cambridge|year=2011|edition=2nd|page=349-352}}</ref>

This handles of a Brownian sheet in the case <math>d=1</math>.  For higher dimensional <math>d</math>, the construction is similar.
